passed.title: pl.zeros defaults to Float64, not an integer dtype
passed.trap: Habits from `[0] * n` or integer-typed code lead people to expect integer zeros. `pl.zeros` defaults to `dtype=Float64`, so you get `0.0` values, not integers. If you need integer zeros, pass the dtype explicitly, for example `pl.zeros(n, pl.Int32)`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.zeros(3, eager=True)
print(s.dtype, s.to_list())

s_int = pl.zeros(3, pl.Int32, eager=True)
print(s_int.dtype, s_int.to_list())

passed.title: Adding pl.zeros to an integer column silently turns it into Float64
passed.trap: Because `pl.zeros` produces Float64 by default, an expression like `pl.col("a") + pl.zeros(n)` promotes an integer column to Float64. No error is raised, but the schema changes for everything downstream, including joins, comparisons and writes. Pass a `dtype` that matches the column you combine it with.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})

bad = df.with_columns(pl.col("a") + pl.zeros(3))
good = df.with_columns(pl.col("a") + pl.zeros(3, pl.Int64))

print(bad.schema["a"])
print(good.schema["a"])

passed.title: pl.zeros returns an Expr unless eager=True
passed.trap: The default is `eager=False`, so `pl.zeros(3)` returns a lazy `pl.Expr`, not data. Calling `Series` methods such as `Series.to_list` on it fails. Pass `eager=True` to get a `pl.Series`, or evaluate the expression with `pl.select`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

z = pl.zeros(3)
print(isinstance(z, pl.Expr), isinstance(z, pl.Series))
try:
    z.to_list()
except AttributeError:
    print("AttributeError")

s = pl.zeros(3, eager=True)
print(isinstance(s, pl.Series), s.to_list())

print(pl.select(pl.zeros(3)).to_series().to_list())

note.title: A fixed n must equal the frame height; use pl.lit to broadcast
note.trap: `pl.zeros(n)` builds a column of exactly `n` rows. If `n` differs from the height of the frame you add it to, `DataFrame.with_columns` raises an error instead of broadcasting. Hard-coding `n` also breaks as soon as the data size changes. Use `pl.lit` when you do not need a predetermined length, because a scalar literal broadcasts to the frame height.
note.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3, 4]})

try:
    df.with_columns(pl.zeros(3).alias("z"))
    print("no error")
except Exception:
    print("raised an error")

good = df.with_columns(pl.lit(0.0).alias("z"))
print(good)

note.title: The output column is named zeros, so it neither replaces your column nor coexists with a second zeros
note.trap: The result of `pl.zeros` is named `zeros`. Putting it in `DataFrame.with_columns` adds a new column called `zeros` and leaves your existing column untouched. Two unaliased `pl.zeros` calls in one `DataFrame.with_columns` produce duplicate output names and raise an error. Always use `Expr.alias` to name the target column.
note.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2]})

out = df.with_columns(pl.zeros(2))
print(out.columns)

try:
    df.with_columns(pl.zeros(2), pl.zeros(2, pl.Int64))
    print("no error")
except Exception:
    print("raised an error")

fixed = df.with_columns(pl.zeros(2, pl.Int64).alias("x"))
print(fixed)
